scenes.title: COLD OPEN — The Night the Water Left
scenes.setting: The old ocean, mid-Withdrawal; then a century of the same coastline in dissolves; ending on present-day Saltwick Light.
scenes.palette: moonlit indigo / salt-white ebb, ink horizon
scenes.music: a single held low string under wind; no melody yet; the score itself seems to withdraw with the water
sfx: vast receding hiss of water leaving
hulls groaning onto wet sand
wind over salt
one distant lamp mechanism ticking
scenes.action: Open already inside the catastrophe: a moonlit ocean is walking out of the world, the water sliding backward in one continuous silver sheet, moon-path stretching and snapping like pulled taffy. By fifteen seconds, fishing ships keel over into gleaming wet sand, masts tilting in silhouette, anchor chains left pointing at nothing. FRAME ONE (to be reprised): the sea's retreating edge seen from the cliff, a bright line abandoning the land. Three narration cards burn in over black between images. Then a century pours through dissolves on a locked-off wide: the harbor dries and whitens, salt crystals climb the dead hulls like frost in fast-motion, kelp forests petrify into verdigris stone, whale bones surface from the flats like the ribs of the world, and a town retreats up its cliff one rooftop at a time. FRAME TWO: a lone lamp burning on the cliff edge at night while the darkness below seems to LEAN toward it, a shade too deep, deep like depth. End present day — FRAME THREE: Saltwick Light's beam sweeps slow across a sea of air, and everywhere the beam is not, the black underneath reads as black that still moves like the sea being water.

dialogue.speaker: NARRATION
dialogue.line: A hundred years ago, in one night, the sea left.
dialogue.note: card 1, over the water walking out

dialogue.speaker: NARRATION
dialogue.line: The law says every light burns till dawn.
dialogue.note: card 2, over the lone lamp and the leaning dark

dialogue.speaker: NARRATION
dialogue.line: Nobody remembers why.
dialogue.note: card 3, over the beam sweeping emptiness

scenes.title: TITLE CARD
scenes.music: silence except wind; one struck-glass tone as the letters finish growing
sfx: beam sweep whoosh into whiteout
crystalline crackle of salt growing
one small bell, very far away, rung once
scenes.action: The lighthouse beam swings directly into camera — whiteout. Out of the white, black returns first, and then letters grow across it the way salt takes a hull: branching crystal, faintly blue at the edges, resolving into SALTGLASS and beneath it, smaller, KEEP THE LIGHT. Hold on the finished title in silence. Then, from somewhere impossibly far out on the flats, one small bell rings once — and the letters give a single faint pulse of blue before we cut.

scenes.title: Low Tide of a Hundred Years
scenes.setting: The Dry Sea beneath Saltwick Light: stone kelp under a whale ribcage; then the lamp room at breakfast.
scenes.palette: gold dawn / bone-white flats, kelp verdigris
scenes.music: warm sparse guitar-and-glass motif — the household theme, played light
sfx: chisel taps on stone kelp
brass signal bell: two clean rings
kettle rattle and catch
gulls that are not gulls — dry-flats birds
scenes.action: Golden light rakes the seabed and every whale rib throws a shadow a hundred meters long. Under the ribcage, small and utterly unafraid, Espen chisels a nub of blue saltglass out of a stone kelp stalk, breath fogging, tongue between his teeth. Close-up: the crystal drops into a jar half full of blue fragments — they clink like ice. Far above, tiny on the cliff, Saltwick Light's brass signal bell swings twice: their private language. Espen rolls his eyes, pockets the jar, and takes the cliff stair two at a time in silhouette. LAMP ROOM: breakfast laid out under the great lens, the dead lamp huge and museum-still behind them. Orla's salt-stiff hand loses the kettle mid-pour — both her hands snap together and catch it, an old practiced save; Espen sees the save, not the slip. Then, framed clean and center for camera while Espen digs through his jar with his back half turned: Orla unfolds a small paper square and taps white powder into her tea, folds the paper away with two fingers, drinks. The scene ends on Espen pocketing the jar in silent protest, and her watching him not watch her.

dialogue.speaker: ORLA
dialogue.line: You climb like the stairs owe you money.

dialogue.speaker: ESPEN
dialogue.line: You ring like the bell owes you dinner.

dialogue.speaker: ORLA
dialogue.line: Two rings means food. You came up on one and a half.

dialogue.speaker: ESPEN
dialogue.line: Found a whole vein of blue under the third rib. Look at it.

dialogue.speaker: ORLA
dialogue.line: Mm. The sea's old teeth.

dialogue.speaker: ESPEN
dialogue.line: It's salt with a mood, Gran.

dialogue.speaker: ORLA
dialogue.line: Everything down there is something with a mood.

dialogue.speaker: ESPEN
dialogue.line: I had it.
dialogue.note: after the kettle save

dialogue.speaker: ORLA
dialogue.line: You had the floor. The floor had the kettle.

dialogue.speaker: ESPEN
dialogue.line: Your hands okay?

dialogue.speaker: ORLA
dialogue.line: My hands are seventy. Ask them nothing before noon.
dialogue.note: deflection; she pours anyway

dialogue.speaker: ESPEN
dialogue.line: Hulda's caravan goes out after storm season.

dialogue.speaker: ORLA
dialogue.line: So does every fool with two legs and no roof to mind.

dialogue.speaker: ESPEN
dialogue.line: If I sell the whole jar, I can get the wheel. The good one. With spokes.

dialogue.speaker: ORLA
dialogue.line: Oil first.

dialogue.speaker: ESPEN
dialogue.line: It's always oil first. We eat oil. We dream oil.

dialogue.speaker: ORLA
dialogue.line: When you keep a lamp, you'll count different.

dialogue.speaker: ESPEN
dialogue.line: I don't keep a lamp. I carry stairs for one.

dialogue.speaker: ORLA
dialogue.line: Then carry the can to Hulda's. Full weight, and watch her thumb.

dialogue.speaker: ESPEN
dialogue.line: Her thumb weighs a fish.

dialogue.speaker: ORLA
dialogue.line: So does your excuse.

scenes.title: Hulda's Scales
scenes.setting: Cliff-town market street; Hulda's oil stall under a rust-red awning; the cliff rail overlooking the strait.
scenes.palette: chalk noon / laundry white, rust awnings, hazed strait
scenes.music: the household theme gone dry and plucked — bored, sun-bleached; drops out entirely at the jar pulse
sfx: laundry snapping in wind
brass scale pans clinking
one coin sliding on skin
a single soft glass hum — the jar pulse
scenes.action: Noon flattens the town to chalk and shadow: laundry lines cross the street like signal flags, a cat sleeps in a dry boat planter. At her stall Hulda — big, sun-cured, thumb permanently at home on the scale — pokes through Espen's tray of trinkets while the oil can waits on the counter between them. Close-up: brass scale pans, trinkets on one side, coins on the other, her thumb resting just so. When she counts out the oil money, Espen's hand palms one coin off the top mid-pass — a card-trick move, shot tight and unmistakable, the coin vanishing into the same pocket as the jar. They walk together to the cliff rail; Hulda squints across the strait where a smudge of haze sits on the horizon exactly where a tower should be. Espen leans on the rail, bored. In his pocket, framed in a tight insert: the jar gives one slow blue pulse, lighting the coin beside it. He pulls it out, taps it against the rail like a dead watch, shrugs, and walks on — and behind him, unwatched, it pulses once more toward the strait.

dialogue.speaker: HULDA
dialogue.line: Kelp glass, bone buttons... and what is this, a saint's toe?

dialogue.speaker: ESPEN
dialogue.line: Whale ear-stone. Worth your whole awning, probably.

dialogue.speaker: HULDA
dialogue.line: Probably. The word I pay least for.

dialogue.speaker: HULDA
dialogue.line: Oil's up again. Storm season. Everything true costs more in storm season.

dialogue.speaker: ESPEN
dialogue.line: Gran says full weight.

dialogue.speaker: HULDA
dialogue.line: Your gran says a lot of hundred-year-old things.

dialogue.speaker: HULDA
dialogue.line: A century, boy. Not one ship. Not a rowboat. Not a duck.

dialogue.speaker: HULDA
dialogue.line: And she burns coin every night to warn them.

dialogue.speaker: ESPEN
dialogue.line: Yeah.

dialogue.speaker: HULDA
dialogue.line: Yeah?
dialogue.note: she actually looks up

dialogue.speaker: ESPEN
dialogue.line: It's a museum. She's the exhibit.
dialogue.note: grinning; first time out loud

dialogue.speaker: HULDA
dialogue.line: Ha! Ten years I've said it. First time a keeper's blood agreed with me.

dialogue.speaker: ESPEN
dialogue.line: Apprentice. It's different.

dialogue.speaker: HULDA
dialogue.line: Not in the ledger it isn't.

dialogue.speaker: HULDA
dialogue.line: Spring caravan. There's still a place, if your legs are serious.
dialogue.note: as the coin disappears

dialogue.speaker: ESPEN
dialogue.line: I asked, didn't I?

dialogue.speaker: HULDA
dialogue.line: You asked like a boy buying something behind his gran's back.

dialogue.speaker: ESPEN
dialogue.line: It's my back.

dialogue.speaker: HULDA
dialogue.line: Funny. Can't see Farholm's tower lately.
dialogue.note: squinting across the strait

dialogue.speaker: ESPEN
dialogue.line: It's noon.

dialogue.speaker: HULDA
dialogue.line: At noon you see the tower. Haze, probably.

dialogue.speaker: ESPEN
dialogue.line: Cheap junk.
dialogue.note: to himself, tapping the jar like a dead watch

scenes.title: The Lesson — Six Minutes
scenes.setting: The lamp room at dusk: the great lens, the match tin, the stove ledge, the cracked pane.
scenes.palette: ember dusk / brass, oil-flame amber, one cracked pane of storm-green
scenes.music: a slow six-note figure enters under the litany — one note per minute-rule; it will become the setpiece clock
sfx: wick scissors snip
oil filling to a ring
match tin rattle — eight loose matches
wind whistling thin through the cracked pane
scenes.action: Dusk turns the lamp room to embers and brass. The whole ritual is taught in close-ups of hands: Orla's — salt-cracked, knuckles like rope knots — trimming the wick, wiping the ring, laying the tin open; Espen's beside them, young and quick and half-hearted, mimicking each motion a beat late, fingers busy spinning the saltglass jar between steps. One pane in the storm-side glass carries a hairline crack that whistles; the wind through it flutters a rag she has stuffed in the gap. She points at it; he shrugs; the shrug is shot as clearly as the crack. Insert: the tin — eight matches, counted with her thumb. Insert: the stove ledge, its wood worn pale in exactly a tin-sized rectangle from a century of matches drying there overnight; Espen pockets the tin instead, still damp from the seabed morning, and the empty pale rectangle holds the frame for one long beat. Then the scene breaks pattern: her hand closes on his wrist, hard, older-strong, and she guides his fingers behind the great lens to a small brass clip where one match rests alone. The last shot is her face lit half by dusk, stopping herself at the edge of a sentence.

dialogue.speaker: ORLA
dialogue.line: Hands.

dialogue.speaker: ORLA
dialogue.line: Softer than mine were at eight. Never mind. Watch.

dialogue.speaker: ORLA
dialogue.line: Minute one: shut the pane. Wind is a thief with patient fingers.

dialogue.speaker: ESPEN
dialogue.line: The pane's fine.

dialogue.speaker: ORLA
dialogue.line: The pane is cracked and you've been told twice.

dialogue.speaker: ESPEN
dialogue.line: It whistles. I like the whistle.

dialogue.speaker: ORLA
dialogue.line: Minute two: trim the wick. Black beard, no flame.

dialogue.speaker: ORLA
dialogue.line: Minute three: oil to the ring. Not past it, not shy of it.

dialogue.speaker: ORLA
dialogue.line: Minute four: dry hands, dry matches. Say it.

dialogue.speaker: ESPEN
dialogue.line: Dry hands, dry matches.
dialogue.note: flat, humoring her

dialogue.speaker: ORLA
dialogue.line: Say it like it's yours.

dialogue.speaker: ESPEN
dialogue.line: Dry hands. Dry matches.

dialogue.speaker: ORLA
dialogue.line: Minute five: strike away from your body.

dialogue.speaker: ORLA
dialogue.line: Minute six: burn.

dialogue.speaker: ESPEN
dialogue.line: And if it doesn't?

dialogue.speaker: ESPEN
dialogue.line: Gran. What happens at minute seven?
dialogue.note: into her silence

dialogue.speaker: ORLA
dialogue.line: The tin holds eight. Buy more tomorrow.
dialogue.note: not an answer, and both know it

dialogue.speaker: ORLA
dialogue.line: Matches sleep on the stove ledge. Every night. Even when I don't.

dialogue.speaker: ESPEN
dialogue.line: Six minutes. It's a lamp, not a heart.
dialogue.note: pocketing the damp tin

dialogue.speaker: ORLA
dialogue.line: Behind the great lens. One spare. Dry.
dialogue.note: gripping his wrist, out of character

dialogue.speaker: ESPEN
dialogue.line: Ow— fine. One spare. For what?

dialogue.speaker: ORLA
dialogue.line: For the night the tin lies to you.

scenes.title: The Ledger and the Storm Supper
scenes.setting: The keeper's kitchen below the lamp room; window on the strait where the storm builds.
scenes.palette: storm-green horizon / lantern amber interior, charcoal cloudwall
scenes.music: household theme, fullest and warmest statement — deliberately held long, cello under it for the first time
sfx: pages of the ledger turning, dry as leaves
storm building far off — pressure, not thunder yet
spoon on bowl
paper square folding: three small creases
scenes.action: Lantern amber inside; through the window, the storm assembles over the strait like a black wall being bricked up in real time, beautiful and enormous. Espen makes his announcement standing, braced for a fight that never comes. Instead Orla slides the keeper's ledger across the table: a century of nightly entries, the handwriting changing every few pages as one dead relative hands the pen to the next — the last pages hers, and the last lines of hers visibly shakier than the first. Close-up: Espen's finger stops on a misspelled entry; the smallest genuine smile passes between them. Supper: she lands her joke; he laughs — a real one, caught in profile against the storm-lit window, the episode's warmest single frame. Then, while his back is turned to fetch bowls: insert of the paper square unfolding over her tea — empty except for a last dust of white she taps out to nothing. She folds the empty paper and puts it away as carefully as if it were still full. The scene ends on the old world's last image: from Espen's dark bedroom doorway, Orla's small silhouette climbing toward the burning lamp, one hand on the rail, resting once.

dialogue.speaker: ESPEN
dialogue.line: I told Hulda yes. The spring caravan.

dialogue.speaker: ESPEN
dialogue.line: ...You're supposed to yell now.

dialogue.speaker: ORLA
dialogue.line: Am I. Whose lungs are you volunteering?

dialogue.speaker: ORLA
dialogue.line: Then sign out properly when you go. Keepers sign.
dialogue.note: sliding the ledger across

dialogue.speaker: ESPEN
dialogue.line: I'm not a keeper.

dialogue.speaker: ORLA
dialogue.line: Everyone in that book said that once.

dialogue.speaker: ESPEN
dialogue.line: This name's spelled wrong.

dialogue.speaker: ORLA
dialogue.line: Your great-great-uncle. Spelled everything wrong. Kept forty years anyway.

dialogue.speaker: ESPEN
dialogue.line: Forty years of this?

dialogue.speaker: ORLA
dialogue.line: Forty years of dawns. You only ever count the nights.

dialogue.speaker: ESPEN
dialogue.line: The storm looks like a wall.
dialogue.note: at the window

dialogue.speaker: ORLA
dialogue.line: It is a wall. Ours just burns brighter.

dialogue.speaker: ESPEN
dialogue.line: That doesn't mean anything.

dialogue.speaker: ORLA
dialogue.line: Most true things don't. Till they do.

dialogue.speaker: ORLA
dialogue.line: Eat. If the wind takes you, I want it to strain.
dialogue.note: he actually laughs

dialogue.speaker: ORLA
dialogue.line: Bed. If the bell rings, it rings for you.

dialogue.speaker: ESPEN
dialogue.line: It never rings at night.

dialogue.speaker: ORLA
dialogue.line: No. It never does.

scenes.title: The Bell Rings Wrong
scenes.setting: Espen's black bedroom; the spiral stair in storm; the landing below the lamp room.
scenes.palette: wet slate / lightning white, black spiral stair
scenes.music: none — the broken bell IS the music cue; score stays out until scene 8's litany begins
sfx: signal bell ringing wrong: dragged, irregular, stopping mid-swing
stair door banging
rain climbing the spiral like something crawling
her breath, shallow and timed wrong
scenes.action: Black frame. The signal bell — but wrong: dragged, arrhythmic, a hand losing its grip on their language mid-word. Espen's eye opens in the dark before the rest of him. He takes the spiral stair barefoot into weather: the stair door has blown open and rain is climbing the steps in gusts, each lightning flash printing the spiral in white then taking it away. On the landing: Orla, down, one hand still tangled in the bell rope above her like a climber who almost held. He gets under her arm; she is impossibly heavy the way only fallen people are; his feet slide on wet stone. Then the single tilt-up that breaks the night open: past her shoulder, up the last turn of stairs, the lamp room stands DARK — and in a lightning flash the cracked pane shows its rag blown inward, the crack whistling triumphantly. Her face is half in shadow; her subtitled words come in fragments between the wrong breaths. On her last word, thunder lands directly overhead, and Espen looks up the dark spiral alone.

dialogue.speaker: ESPEN
dialogue.line: Gran? Gran—

dialogue.speaker: ESPEN
dialogue.line: Okay. Up. Come on, up— why are you heavy, you weigh nothing—

dialogue.speaker: ORLA
dialogue.line: Pane.
dialogue.note: she doesn't ask how the flame died; she knows

dialogue.speaker: ESPEN
dialogue.line: I know. I know, I'm sorry, I'll fix it, just stand—

dialogue.speaker: ORLA
dialogue.line: Light first.

dialogue.speaker: ESPEN
dialogue.line: You're on the floor!

dialogue.speaker: ORLA
dialogue.line: Then me.

dialogue.speaker: ESPEN
dialogue.line: Gran—

dialogue.speaker: ORLA
dialogue.line: Count.

dialogue.speaker: ORLA
dialogue.line: Count.
dialogue.note: quieter; it is the last thing she has strength for

scenes.title: SETPIECE — Six Minutes of the Wrong Sea
scenes.setting: The dark lamp room; the gallery glass; the Dry Sea filling with darkness below. Intercuts: the landing, the village windows.
scenes.palette: abyssal black / saltglass blue, match-flare orange, cold fin-light rows
scenes.music: the six-note litany figure, one note per minute, degrading as matches die; FULL SCORE DROPOUT when the eye arrives; returns as a single sustained tone with the spare match
sfx: match heads crumbling wet — a sound like sand
the eighth match snapping
rain going SIDEWAYS against glass — current, not weather
hull-creaks through stone, fathoms down
frost blooming: a fine crystalline hiss
one whale-deep note sinking as the light returns
scenes.action: Near-real-time. Espen works the litany aloud — the only clock we get. MINUTE ONE: he jams the rag and his own balled jacket into the cracked pane; wind fights him for it. MINUTE TWO, THREE: wick, oil, hands doing her motions — and in tight inserts his shaking fingers become an exact match of hers from scene 5, knuckle for knuckle. MINUTE FOUR: the tin. The first match head crumbles wet against the striker like sand. The second. The third. He shelters the tin in his shirt; four, five, six, seven die — seven small deaths in close-up, each dud laid on the sill in a lengthening row. MINUTE FIVE: the eighth snaps unstruck between his fingers. And the world changes: the jar on the floor wakes, brightening from ember-blue to drowned-noon-blue; the rain outside stops falling DOWN and streams SIDEWAYS across the gallery glass like current; a long hull-creak rolls up through the tower from ten fathoms of stone below. The score drops out entirely. Outside, rows of faint cold fin-lights rise past the glass, huge and slow, and one eye the size of the supper table comes level with the boy — never centered in frame, never lit, its breath rendered as frost blooming across the pane toward his hand, which recoils. The cold open's three frames return, wider, heavier: the sea coming back wrong; the dark leaning at a lone dead lamp; emptiness where a beam should be. Intercut pressure valves: Orla's hand slack in the bell rope two floors down; the village's lit windows floating in the risen dark like buoys, and going out one by one as people sleep. Then he stops looking at the eye and looks at the lens — remembers her HANDS, not her words — and reaches behind the great lens to the brass clip: one match, dry as a kept promise. He shields it inside her hanging coat, strikes it away from his body on the lens frame, and at the count of six the wick catches. The beam slams outward and the darkness recoils from it like surf off rock — dry land, restored. One whale-deep note sinks below the cliff and does not come back. RENDER RULE: every frame carries an internal light source — jar glow, match flare, lightning rim, fin-light, beam; blacks never crush.

dialogue.speaker: ESPEN

scenes.title: Holding the Line
scenes.setting: The lit lamp room; the six steps of stair between it and the daybed where he settles Orla.
scenes.time_of_day: deep night after the storm's worst
scenes.palette: deep night / single flame gold, blue jar-glow on grey blankets
scenes.music: the six-note litany figure returns intact, gentle now — it has become a lullaby without changing a note
sfx: wick feeding: soft oil sputter
heels dragging on stone, inches at a time
the lamp mechanism wound and ticking
rain thinning to drips
scenes.action: The rest of the night compressed into dissolves paced on the count: Espen feeds the wick — six steps down — drags Orla toward the daybed by inches, her arm over his shoulders, both of them small in the stairwell — six steps up — back before the mechanism runs down. Again. Again. The rhythm the litany was built to teach is now simply how he moves. He gets her onto the daybed, tucks the grey blanket wrong and then fixes it, and sets the saltglass jar — dim now, exhausted-blue — on her windowsill like a night-light, angling it the way you angle a candle for a sick child. She surfaces once, from somewhere far under, and her stiff fingers find the jar's glass. What she says, she says with her eyes closed. When he starts his question the camera is already drifting off her face; asleep, or pretending, and the difference is hers to keep. He climbs back up into the gold. Last shot: the boy sitting where she always sat, lips moving, counting.

dialogue.speaker: ESPEN
dialogue.line: Six down. Six up. That's the whole song, isn't it.

dialogue.speaker: ORLA
dialogue.line: Kettle... had further to fall.
dialogue.note: a joke, from the floor of herself

dialogue.speaker: ESPEN
dialogue.line: Don't joke. You're not allowed to joke on a floor.

dialogue.speaker: ORLA
dialogue.line: Your grandfather kept weather in jars too.
dialogue.note: fingers on the saltglass

dialogue.speaker: ORLA
dialogue.line: He never believed it either. Then he did.

dialogue.speaker: ESPEN
dialogue.line: Gran. The thing at the glass. Its eye was—

dialogue.speaker: ESPEN
dialogue.line: Gran?

dialogue.speaker: ESPEN
dialogue.line: Fine. Sleep. I've got the count.

scenes.title: Dawn — Seven Dead Soldiers
scenes.setting: The lamp room sill and daybed corner, morning after.
scenes.palette: steam-gold dawn / grey blanket, black matchsticks on white sill
scenes.music: household theme returns, but re-voiced on the litany's instruments — the two themes are one theme now
sfx: seabed steaming: a soft white-noise shimmer
teacup on saucer, trembling then steadied
the lamp, still burning, ticking down
scenes.action: The storm is gone and the seabed steams gold from horizon to horizon — for one cruel held beat, through the gallery glass, the vapor moves like swell and it is almost, almost water. Then a bird walks on it and the illusion dies. The night is recapped without a word of narration, in objects: seven burnt matchsticks lined on the white sill like little black soldiers; the snapped eighth laid crosswise beside the empty tin; the lamp above them still burning into daylight. Orla, propped on the daybed, reads the sill the way other people read a letter. Then her stiff hand goes behind the great lens — the clip is empty — and closes slowly on nothing, and that closing hand is the whole conversation. Espen pours her tea; his hand shakes with the specific tremor of a boy who has been awake all night being brave; her salt-stiff hand comes up under the cup and steadies it, the same save as the kettle, offered instead of hidden. Two lines each, and the apprenticeship is signed.

dialogue.speaker: ORLA
dialogue.line: Seven.
dialogue.note: reading the sill

dialogue.speaker: ESPEN
dialogue.line: Eight. One snapped.

dialogue.speaker: ORLA
dialogue.line: Snapped counts.
dialogue.note: the closest she will come to saying you nearly died

dialogue.speaker: ESPEN
dialogue.line: I'll buy more matches.

dialogue.speaker: ORLA
dialogue.line: Buy two tins.

dialogue.speaker: ESPEN
dialogue.line: And putty. For the pane.

dialogue.speaker: ORLA
dialogue.line: I know.
dialogue.note: meaning: I know everything, and it's forgiven

scenes.title: Bells Before Body — The Bellfarer
scenes.setting: The village street at first light; Hulda's stall; the cliff stair where the Dry Sea meets the town; Saltwick Light's beam across the ground.
scenes.palette: shell-pink flats / long blue shadows, bell-brass glints
scenes.music: none under the bells — the bells are the cue; a low sustained note enters under the stanza
sfx: dozens of small bells rising from the seabed, arrhythmic, getting closer
shutters opening along the street
one coin pressed into a palm
oil poured back: a full measure
the cracked bell: a dead clack where a ring should be
scenes.action: Sound arrives before anything else: small bells, many of them, arrhythmic, rising from below the cliff — in a world where the dark listens, a crosser is a lit lamp made of noise. Shutters open down the street; the village leans out in nightclothes. Espen, already up and carrying the oil can, stops at Hulda's stall and presses the skimmed coin into her palm — shot exactly like the skim in scene 4, reversed. She looks at it, then at him, says nothing about it, and while he asks his prices she tips a full extra measure of oil back into his can, thumb nowhere near the scale. Then the Bellfarer crests the cliff stair: wide flat hat, long coat sewn all over with small bells that shiver silent as he stops — and he stops precisely where Saltwick Light's beam meets the ground, boots an inch outside it, like a man honoring a border. He holds his news up as an object first: a small bell, cracked through, salt-fogged white, hung on a cut cord. When he finally looks up, he looks past Hulda, past Orla's window where a grey figure watches, to the boy standing in front of the still-burning lamp. Espen's answer is framed in the wide: small boy, huge tower, lit lamp, rising sun — and the jar in his pocket giving one steady pulse toward the strait.

dialogue.speaker: ESPEN
dialogue.line: Hulda.

dialogue.speaker: HULDA
dialogue.line: It's dawn, boy. Dawn is for bakers and regrets.

dialogue.speaker: HULDA
dialogue.line: What's this?
dialogue.note: the coin in her palm

dialogue.speaker: ESPEN
dialogue.line: Change. From yesterday. Your scale was off.

dialogue.speaker: HULDA
dialogue.line: My scale is never off.

dialogue.speaker: ESPEN
dialogue.line: Then I was.

dialogue.speaker: ESPEN
dialogue.line: What does a month of oil cost? Full weight.

dialogue.speaker: HULDA
dialogue.line: More than a bicycle wheel.
dialogue.note: she has always known about the wheel

dialogue.speaker: ESPEN
dialogue.line: Two months, then.

dialogue.speaker: HULDA
dialogue.line: Storm keep you up?
dialogue.note: tipping the full measure back, unasked

dialogue.speaker: ESPEN
dialogue.line: Something did.

dialogue.speaker: BELLFARER
dialogue.line: Saltwick Light. Still burning past dawn. Good habit.

dialogue.speaker: BELLFARER
dialogue.line: Three weeks on the flats, out of Farholm. My bells are tired.

dialogue.speaker: ESPEN
dialogue.line: Why bells?

dialogue.speaker: BELLFARER
dialogue.line: So the dark can hear I'm not part of it.

dialogue.speaker: BELLFARER
dialogue.line: Cut this from Farholm's keeper-door. Cold as a drowned man's pocket.
dialogue.note: holding up the cracked bell

dialogue.speaker: BELLFARER
dialogue.line: Where a light forgets its keep,

dialogue.speaker: BELLFARER
dialogue.line: the old sea rises from its sleep.

dialogue.speaker: HULDA
dialogue.line: Farholm's dark? I thought it was haze.

dialogue.speaker: BELLFARER
dialogue.line: It was never haze.

dialogue.speaker: BELLFARER
dialogue.line: Three weeks. Nothing has come down off that cliff. Nothing I heard.

dialogue.speaker: BELLFARER
dialogue.line: Who keeps this one?
dialogue.note: looking past everyone, to the boy

dialogue.speaker: ESPEN
dialogue.line: I do.
dialogue.note: first time in his life; framed against the burning lamp

scenes.action: Full pitiless noon, across the strait: Farholm's tower stands white against white sky — and its lamp-room glass is broken OUTWARD, shards glittering down the tower's flank like spray frozen mid-burst. At the tower's base, its own long noon shadow pools on the salt — and inside that shadow, something is still swimming: the pool's dark edge laps and recoils, laps and recoils, in exactly the rhythm the darkness moved against the lamp-room glass in the six dark minutes. Shadow is water. Safety was never daytime; it was light, and light can be lost. Cut back across the strait: Espen's saltglass jar on the sill, glowing steady now, not pulsing — a compass needle, pointed at Farholm. One narration card, the episode's only closing line, over the jar. Then the title re-crystallizes in salt on black; one far bell rings once; black.

dialogue.speaker: NARRATION
dialogue.line: The law says every light burns till dawn. Now you know why.
dialogue.note: single closing card, bookending the cold open
